Name: mechanism_intervention_probing
Title: Do Scientific Foundation Models Encode Mechanisms or Just Correlates? A Causal Intervention Probing Framework
Short Hypothesis: If a foundation model has internalized an established scientific mechanism (e.g., a mutation destabilizes a protein by breaking a hydrophobic-core packing constraint), then intervening on the internal representation of the mechanistic variable should shift the model's output in the direction and (approximate) magnitude predicted by the scientific law — not merely correlate with it. We hypothesize that current biology/chemistry foundation models encode many scientific *correlates* that pass standard probing tests but fail counterfactual mechanistic-intervention tests, and that the fraction of mechanisms that pass is a measurable, informative property of a model.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work on scientific foundation models (Vig et al. 'BERTology Meets Biology'; Murakami et al. SAE for nanobody thermostability; ifDEEPre; ReCLIP) demonstrates that attention heads and sparse-autoencoder features *correlate* with known biological structures (binding sites, hydrophobic core, disulfides, motifs). These are observational/correlational analyses: they show a feature co-occurs with a scientific concept. Our proposal differs fundamentally by adopting a causal-interventional stance borrowed from mechanistic interpretability (activation patching, causal mediation) but reframed around *scientific mechanisms with quantitative laws*. Rather than asking 'does a feature light up at binding sites?', we ask 'does editing the internal variable that the law says is causal produce the law-predicted counterfactual change in output?'. This turns qualitative interpretability into a falsifiable, quantitative test grounded in established mechanisms, and yields a model-agnostic 'mechanism fidelity score' not present in prior work.
Abstract: Foundation models for biology and chemistry make strikingly accurate predictions, and a growing interpretability literature shows their internal features correlate with known scientific concepts such as binding sites, hydrophobic cores, and reaction motifs. But correlation is not mechanism: a model may exploit shortcuts that co-occur with a scientific variable rather than represent the causal law itself. We introduce a causal intervention probing framework that distinguishes representing a mechanism from representing a correlate. For each established mechanism with a known quantitative or directional law (e.g., core hydrophobicity->stability, GC content->mRNA stability, aromaticity->reaction reactivity, charge-charge distance->binding), we (1) locate the internal direction encoding the mechanistic variable via a linear probe, (2) perform activation edits that increase/decrease that variable, and (3) measure whether the model's output changes in the law-predicted direction and magnitude, comparing against a matched non-causal correlate control. We define a Mechanism Fidelity Score aggregating direction agreement, monotonicity, and effect-size calibration. We apply this to open protein (ESM-2), molecular (a public chemistry transformer), and small physics/materials models across ~10 curated mechanisms, using held-out perturbation datasets (deep mutational scans, mRNA stability, reaction yield) as ground truth. We predict a spectrum: some mechanisms are causally encoded and edit-controllable, while others pass probing but fail intervention. The framework provides a reproducible, cheap, model-agnostic tool to audit whether scientific foundation models 'understand' mechanisms, informing trust, model selection, and hypothesis generation.
Experiments: 1. Mechanism curation: Assemble ~10 established mechanisms across domains, each with (a) a directional/quantitative law, (b) a labeled mechanistic variable computable from inputs, and (c) an experimental counterfactual dataset. Examples: hydrophobic-core burial->folding stability (ProTherm/FireProtDB, MegaScale ddG); disulfide presence->stability; charge-pair distance->binding affinity (SKEMPI); GC content/codon usage->mRNA stability (public mRNA stability sets); ring aromaticity->reactivity and Hammett sigma->reaction rate (chemistry datasets); bandgap vs. composition electronegativity (Materials Project). 2. Probe localization: For each model layer, fit linear probes to predict the mechanistic variable from residue/token/atom representations; select the layer/direction with best probe R^2. 3. Correlate controls: For each mechanism, identify a confound variable that correlates in-distribution but is causally irrelevant per the law; fit its probe direction too. 4. Causal edits: Add alpha*direction to activations at the localized layer (activation steering) sweeping alpha; also test activation patching from paired sequences differing only in the mechanistic variable. Measure output shift (predicted stability/affinity/yield). 5. Metrics: Mechanism Fidelity Score = combination of (i) sign-agreement rate between edit-induced output change and law prediction, (ii) monotonicity/Spearman of output vs. alpha, (iii) calibration slope of edit effect vs. experimentally measured counterfactual effect. Compare mechanistic-direction edits to correlate-control edits and to random-direction edits (null). 6. Cross-model comparison: Run across model sizes (ESM-2 8M->650M) to test whether mechanism fidelity scales. 7. Validation: For mechanisms that pass, verify with real experimental counterfactual pairs (single-mutant DMS) that edit magnitude tracks measured effect; for failing mechanisms, show the model relies on the correlate via correlate-edit sensitivity. 8. Deliverable: open benchmark of mechanisms + fidelity leaderboard across public models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Linear-probe localization may miss nonlinearly encoded mechanisms, causing false negatives; mitigate with multiple layers and nonlinear probes as robustness checks. 2. Activation edits can push representations off-manifold, producing artifactual output changes; mitigate with activation patching from real paired inputs and off-manifold detection. 3. Disentangling a mechanistic variable from correlated confounds may be imperfect when inputs cannot vary them independently; use naturally decorrelated held-out subsets and synthetic sequence pairs. 4. Ground-truth counterfactual datasets are noisy and domain-limited, especially in physics/materials; may restrict some mechanisms to qualitative direction tests. 5. Effect-size calibration depends on output being on a physical scale; for classification-only models we fall back to directional metrics. 6. Results are model- and mechanism-specific and may not generalize, but this specificity is itself the intended diagnostic output.
